[F1 2027 calendar: Monaco GP gets sprint race, Türkiye and Portugal return to schedule] The 2027 Monaco Grand Prix has been named as one of 10 sprint races on next year's 24-race calendar, which includes the return of rounds in Türkiye and Portugal. The 2027 schedule is set to get underway with a sprint race in Bahrain on March 14 and run until the final race of the season in Abu Dhabi on Dec. 12, which will also feature Formula 1's sprint format. The addition of a sprint race in Monaco is among the most unexpected additions to the calendar as the tight street circuit is notorious for its lack of overtaking. Sprint weekends feature just one practice session on Friday followed by sprint qualifying the same day, a sprint race (one third of the length of a full grand prix) on Saturday before the standard qualifying and the grand prix take place on Saturday and Sunday as usual. Sources have indicated to ESPN that Formula 1 believes the addition of a second qualifying session in Monaco will add value over two practice sessions, with the potential for two different grid orders in the sprint and main grand prix. Qualifying has long been seen as the highlight of the Monaco Grand Prix weekend, partly due to the skill required to thread a car between the narrow barriers and partly because it very often defines the finishing order for Sunday's grand prix. The Monaco Grand Prix getting a sprint race is the biggest surprise on the F1 2027 calendar reveal. Photo by Joe Portlock/Getty Images F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali has been keen to increase the number of sprint races in recent years due to the increased viewership the format receives by substituting two extra competitive sessions for two practice sessions. "Data shows that total viewership of Sprint weekends is 12% higher than non-Sprint weekends, Sprint Qualifying is up to three times more popular with fans than Free Practice," F1 said in a press release. messages.content: [2026 Iran war fuel crisis] The 2026 Iran war fuel crisis is a worldwide fuel crisis caused by the war between Iran and the U.S.-Israel coalition. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which over 20% of the world's oil trade passes, and attacks on energy infrastructure in Iran and several Gulf Cooperation Council countries led to a large disruption in global oil supplies. The disruption led to global oil prices rising and caused fuel shortages in countries which imported most of their fuel from the Persian Gulf region. Much of the world has been affected by panic buying and severe disruption to the distribution of petroleum products, liquefied natural gas (LNG), and urea used for fertiliser. The economies of most countries are expected to be adversely affected by the crisis, leading to inflation and heightened risks of stagflation and recession. As of April 2026 there was ongoing concerns about energy security as well as food security, related to fertiliser shortages and costs. Brent prices initially surged to a peak of approximately $118 in late March 2026 before declining to around $70 by July 1, then rebounded to over $100 by late July and fluctuated between $87 and $97 through August. As of early September 2026, price surged up to $109 as renewed attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure reversed earlier gains. By June 2026, the yearly inflation rate is 3.53%, with the consumer price index decreasing by 0.42% and weekly earnings increasing by 0.77% since May 2026. In July, the IMF revised its world GDP growth rate to 3% for 2026 and 3.4% in 2027. According to IMF the effect of the oil supply shock on the world economy is limited due to the AI-driven demand.
